blurb: Eleven days of one production incident: a service that falls over some minutes after every deploy, three wrong theories, two teams, and the log line that finally explained it.

Right, an update, and it is not the one I wanted. Something I should have mentioned earlier and did not think mattered: our deploy rotates the service credentials as its last step. That is 13 minutes before the first failures, give or take, and it lines up better than anything else we have looked at. Laid out in order:

10:00  deploy started
10:04  rolling restart complete
10:04  readiness green on all replicas
10:07  credentials rotated
10:13  first elevated latency
10:15  first client-visible error
10:20  error rate above alert threshold
10:26  manual restart, service recovers

What would you look at next?

I want to be careful with `10:04  readiness green on all replicas`, because it appears on healthy deploys too. On its own it is noise; alongside the rest of what you sent, it is not.

Here is where I think we are, and what I have handed to the identity team along with your logs. Their view of the network layer is better than mine, and the question I have asked them is narrow: whether a rotated credential invalidates connections that are already open.

1. Send me the request ids for three failures and three successes in the same minute — I can trace them from our side and compare.
2. Turn off credential rotation for one deploy only — this is the cheapest way to test the theory and the easiest to undo.
3. Re-run with debug logging on the client only — the server side already has what we need.
4. Set the connection max lifetime below the rotation interval — if this is the cause, the failure disappears entirely.

If the next run behaves differently in any way, send the logs even if it looks like an improvement. An improvement we cannot explain is still a symptom.

The one I keep coming back to is `2026-07-11 22:07:41Z WARN query-planner[pid 1498] req=req-7584 batch=72045 latency=1602ms pool=2`. Read it next to the timestamps in your timeline and the ordering is the wrong way round for the theory we were holding.

What that pattern usually means is that the query-planner is losing its connections one at a time rather than all at once, which is why the failure looks gradual and why restarting clears it. The 3-minute delay is the age of the oldest connection in the pool, not a threshold anywhere in the configuration.

1. Re-run with debug logging on the client only — the server side already has what we need.
2. Capture the pool's in-use count once a second for the whole window — the shape of that curve separates exhaustion from refusal.
3. Keep the rollback in place overnight — we lose a day, and we do not lose the evening.
4. Run the same batch with the pool capped at four connections — if the failure arrives sooner, the age of the connections is the variable.

I will have an answer from the networking team by tomorrow afternoon and I will write here either way, including if the answer is that they need more.

Before anything else: `2026-07-15 16:42:14Z ERROR index-builder[pid 1113] req=req-4623 batch=86571 latency=3165ms pool=`. That is a refusal, not a timeout. The difference matters because a refusal is instant and a timeout is not, and everything in your latency graph is consistent with instant.

What that pattern usually means is that the index-builder is losing its connections one at a time rather than all at once, which is why the failure looks gradual and why restarting clears it. The 6-minute delay is the age of the oldest connection in the pool, not a threshold anywhere in the configuration.

1. Capture the pool's in-use count once a second for the whole window — the shape of that curve separates exhaustion from refusal.
2. Turn off credential rotation for one deploy only — this is the cheapest way to test the theory and the easiest to undo.
3. Set the connection max lifetime below the rotation interval — if this is the cause, the failure disappears entirely.
